I am
glad the minister was able to see that it would be of no use to ask me to apologize, because I have no apologies to offer to anyone. What I said the other night I will repeat, because I believe it and the operation of certain schemes proves it. So do not think you are getting any apology out of me.

Referring to Hansard of
May 31, in which a list of marketing schemes appears, I should like to take this opportunity of putting those schemes in order by parts of the country in order to show how many schemes are in force throughout Canada and in each part of it. That will be most useful for anyone who wants to study the accomplishments of the Department of Agriculture in the last five years and especially in the last few months. *
According to the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture on May 31, in the Dominion of Canada there are only two dominion marketing schemes, the one in connection with fruit exports, dated September 8, 1934, and the other in connection with jam exports, dated April 10, 1935. Those are the only schemes which have dominion application; if I am wrong in that statement I will ask the hon. gentleman to correct me in due course. In British Columbia there are apparently six schemes, but if you analyze them you find that there really are not as many as six. First there is the red cedar shingle export marketing scheme dated October 16, 1934. Next is the tree fruit marketing scheme dated August 28, 1934. Next is the dried salt herring and dried salt salmon marketing scheme, dated October 22, 1934. Then there is the lower mainland milk marketing scheme dated January 1, 1935, which apparently is in force in only a portion of British Columbia. In addition there are two vegetable marketing schemes; first there is the interior vegetable marketing scheme dated March 4, 1935, and then there is the coast vegetable marketing scheme of the same date.	The minister takes that one
scheme and cuts it into two.
There are no schemes in the other western provinces, while in Ontario there are apparently four. First there is the flue cured tobacco marketing scheme dated October 26, 1934. Then there is the western Ontario bean marketing scheme dated February 1, 1935. Then, in addition to the dominion fruit export scheme, there is also a scheme known as the dominion apple marketing scheme, which apparently applies only to Ontario. Since the apple is a good Canadian fruit, I do not see the necessity for a dominion apple
marketing scheme, especially for the province of Ontario when there is a fruit marketing scheme for the whole of Canada. In Ontario there are only two marketing schemes, for tobacco and beans. Eastern Canada has a potato marketing scheme, and that is all there is to it. There is very little in it, but what I am afraid of is that matters might get worse through more schemes coming into force.
May I point out one other thing. This kind of legislation is nefarious. Why? For several reasons, but especially for this reason: The federal Department of Agriculture was created in order to improve trade between the provinces. In every province there is a department of agriculture to look after the interests of the farmers of the province.

regulation may provide for equalization as between the producers of the returns received from the sale of the regulated product.
What is the regulated product? It is the product mentioned in section 1 of this bill. What I complain of in this section relating to equalization is that it is worded in such a way that no one can understand it. I might complain of section 4 because instead of there being an equalization of returns there will be under this legislation a decrease of returns to the farmer who raises any one of the products mentioned in section 1 of this bill. I am strongly opposed to that. The minister is interfering with trade between the provinces. The government has killed the farmer's external trade, and now it proposes to kill his internal trade. I am strongly opposed to that, and particularly because it is done in a misleading way. It is done under the guise of helping the . farmer, leading him to think that he will get some benefits from this legislation when he will get none at all.
Nothing but taxes.

Coming back to the point I was making a moment ago, trade between all the provinces was the main and only reason why the fathers of confederation decided that there should be a federal department of agriculture, in spite of the fact that there was to be a provincial department of agriculture in every one of the provinces then existing or to be created. Every province has now a department of agriculture to look after the interests of the farmers of the province in a parochial way, but the federal Department of Agriculture has in its charge the interests of the farmers of the whole country. The farmers of Nova Scotia have to look to the Minister of Agriculture for the possibility of marketing their products in the other provinces, and the same with the farmers of every other province of Canada. But as my hon. friend from North York (Mr. Mulock) interjects, all the farmers get out of this is taxes. The government is showing them the way. It is leading them to ruin in their domestic trade in natural products.

Last year when I asked the minister for information respecting the decrease in the home consumption of farm products I got no satisfactory reply except this one, which I have already repeated in this house and which I shall repeat again if the session lasts much longer. It was that the Prime Minister was too busy listening to Russia and to Litvinoff to look after such things as our trade. That was the answer given, by the Minister of Agriculture when I was speaking of this very same thing last year. If the Prime Minister is too busy to look after the home consumption of farm products because he is too much occupied in drawing inspiration from the communists of Russia and other parts of Europe-
Order.
You may stop me from speaking, Mr. Chairman, but I have told the truth and I shall not further insist upon it.

I would like to have this clear: Under clause 4 and preceding clauses is it not possible to use the money asked in this vote?
Which vote does the hon. .member mean?

Any
vote. Money that is collected. The only way public money could be used would be through a combination with section 9.

I should like to repeat miy question because I want to be clear on the point. Is that correct?
Yes.
Is it proposed that they re-collect the moneys that were advanced to promote schemes such as the poultry scheme of the western provinces?

No; no money will be advanced under section 3 for the promotion or organization of schemes. That is already provided for. But there has been no provision by which money could be obtained by a board until it got under way.

I am back to my original point. For the sake of argument, after a tomato board gets under way and before the producers under the scheme have begun to reap the benefits of the scheme-in other words until they have begun to receive funds from the sale of their product which, under the scheme, would of course according to the minister be greatly increased-the government is going to aot as a banker to advance money to the local board until such time as their own revenues come in. Is that right?
Yes.

My next question is this: It is clearly set out 'that the government undertakes to became banker for these local boards set up under the Natural Products Marketing Act, until such time as they collect from their own producers the toll per bushel or per acre or whatever it is set by the local board under the authority of the federal board. Until the funds come in the government is the banker. That is, they anticipate that they are going to receive a price or be able to sell the product and that the funds will come in. If they do not come in it will be the old story. The next question I wish to have answered is this: Is the government taking power under this bill to use public moneys for the equalization of the price of a natural product under any scheme, local or otherwise?
It might be so used, yes-by using section 9.

This committee is to understand that we are taking one .more step towards national socialism, or fascism, whichever you call it; we are going to take public moneys received from a sugar tax or some other tax and use it to equalize the price of cheese, hags or something else. That is the way I understand the minister's answer. That, I believe, is the answer he intended to give and the answer justified by the bill. It brings us to this point: In Ontario, for instance, we are under a tomato scheme. We are going to can tomatoes under a local board. Canners will pay the price of the local board and if it is sanctioned by the federal board w,e will use public moneys or
Marketing Act Amendment

public taxes to equalize ithe price of tomatoes in a certain area. But, sir, what happens in British Columbia or Quebec? They say, "We have no local scheme or local board, and we are going to sell our tomatoes to 'the canning factories at twenty-five cents a bushel." The price is stabilized at thirty cents in Northumberland county, or some other point in Ontario, and the government has power to use the taxpayers' money to equalize the price of tomatoes under a local marketing scheme in Ontario. Our far-seeing brothers across the Quebec border-I have seen it more than once; I have been .through it, and it has cost me plenty of money-say, "Let these bright fellows in Ontario set up a local board; let them establish a price; let them go to the Minister of Agriculture and let him go to his federal .marketing board. He will undoubtedly get the advice developed in an aoademic mind that the proper thing to do is to use public funds and equalize the price in Ontario." What happens to our bright boys in Quebec? They say, "No, w.e will sell our tomatoes to the canning factories at twenty-five cents, on the open market. We will do as we like on the open market." The canner can get tomatoes in the province of Quebec for less money than he can under a controlled scheme in Ontario, and the result is that the Ontario farmer loses the Montreal and Quebec markets. His Frenich-Canadian brother is wise enough to keep his head out, of these asinine schemes. That is what happens. This is all new to the Minister .of Railways and Canals, who is smiling at me. If it had cost him as much as it has cost me he would be weeping, not smiling.
I am telling you what happens. Let me repeat that if we attempt to do this we will disorganize production in Canada; we will not assist the producers, and we will complicate not only external but internal trade. I give the minister ample credit for having taken his advice from other than intimate officials of the department, but I must say to him that if he continues with these schemes he will disorganize not only internal production but internal distribution and will set up ultraprovincialism within the country. He is making a mistake, and I am pleading with him for that reason.

Tell him about
potatoes.

The
minister knows all about potatoes; I told him two weeks ago that we dumped our potatoes because no one could force anyone else to buy something that he did not want. And that is

what has happened in connection with more than one industry I am associated with. You cannot do certain things and you should not attempt to do them, and this committee should not be asked to vote the money of the Canadian taxpayers to do the impossible. That is my point. They should not be asked to do it because it is wrong. We should not be asked to vote public money in order to dislocate internal production and distribution and to set up ultra-nationalism in this country. If you attempt to do anything of the kind you will find someone a- leap ahead of you. You cannot defy the law of supply and demand-and it is not laissez-faire. You must remember that this is not England where consumption predominates; we are in Canada where production predominates and we must have markets following the natural trend of trade, where individual brains are. pitted against the brains of others. I repeat, it is not a policy of laissez-faire but the unswerving law of supply and demand, the survival of the fittest in business, if you like. We must follow that law in order to get rid of our production internally and externally. Once more I plead with the minister not to take public funds to do something that is impossible.

In our country the only way the producers of beans have of marketing their product is through the elevator. I must register a protest against this section. I said last year, when the Natural Products Marketing Act was under discussion, all that I had to say as to the objections I have against the principle of the legislation, but section 5 of this bill makes still stronger the compulsory features of the legislation to which we object. What I object to more especially is section 14, which is being amended by section 5 of this bill, which is a departure from the ordinary principle that a man is presumed innocent of any offence until he is proved guilty. This is

a new feature altogether. Let me quote the provision:
(2) In any prosecution under this act or under any regulation it shall not be necessary for the prosecuting authority to prove that the product in respect of which the prosecution is instituted was produced within that part of Canada to which the scheme relates, and if the accused person pleads or alleges that the product was not produced within that part of Canada to which the scheme relates, the burden of proof thereof shall be upon the accused person.
What have we come to in this country under this legislation? First of all, farmers may be compulsorily brought under a scheme. The minister says that is only if they want it, but he explains that by saying that it is if the majority wants it, or if the dominion marketing board comes to the conclusion, without a vote, that there is a sufficient majority in favour of the scheme. In that event all the others who are not in favour of the scheme are compulsorily brought under it. Secondly, those who have not voted for it and who are brought under it by compulsion must obey the orders or even the determinations of the dominion board or of the local board or any regulation of the governor in council, and if they do not they will be fined $25 or $500 or go to gaol for three months, or they may be both fined and gaoled. And they are presumed guilty under this bill unless they prove that they are not.
As in Russia.

My hon. friend says, as in Russia, and he is right. These schemes of regimentation can be successful only under a dictatorship. That is the experience. Russia would never have been able to achieve even the small degree of success which she has with her quinquennial plan if she had not the Ogpu, that famous military police. And the same in Germany and Italy. It is the military arm that makes possible the regimentation of the German and Italian farmers under a bureaucratic system of control. But I claim that the Canadian farmers will not submit to it. It is against our mentality. An hon. member says, not in Quebec. Yes; I defy the government to force the Quebec farmers to come under such compulsion. It is against our traditions; it is against the mentality of our people and it cannot be forced. And why pass such bills, which are permanent? In the United States where they have enacted all sorts of laws during the last two years they have had at least the saving clause in ail the preambles to the NRA legislation that it was only for the period of emergency that
then existed, so much so that the NRA was enacted only for two years. It had to be extended this year for a few months, and
everyone knows that President Roosevelt had difficulty in getting that extension. But these acts which this parliament has enacted have not the saving clause that they are to remain in force only during the depression, to meet an emergency; they are permanent. We are putting on the statutes of this country laws which are repugnant to the mentality of the Canadian people, and I agree with one hon. gentleman who spoke to-night, that we have had too many such laws during the last two or three years. I think the main work of the next parliament will be to repeal most of the legislation which has been enacted this year and last. I pray that my hon. friend will not insist on this subsection 2 which will force a man. because he is accused of having disobeyed an order of a local board, mind you, to bring witnesses and incur expense for the purpose of proving that he is not guilty. This should not happen in any civilized country; we should not have such legislation in Canada. I still believe those schemes of bureaucratic regimentation will not be successful in this country. Canadians will remain personalities, individuals; they will not become tools in a machine organized and controlled by some bureaucrat in Ottawa. So far as I am concerned I am going to vote against this section of this bill, and if it remains there, I will vote against this whole bill on third reading.
